utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, I have a slight technical problem, my computer is not functioning. If we can get someone from the technical staff to get me up and running, after the long break. It is still taking a vacation, Judge, the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not used to being busy. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We have a full house. Nobody is absent today. We will like to start the proceedings, as we are scheduled to sit for the next four weeks, in as much as possible we would like to sit uninterrupted, so that we will be able to accomplish things which we have not been able to do during the past three weeks. We intend, except if you have other problems, to extend our sittings to Fridays, although our schedule indicates that we should sit Mondays to Thursdays. But in order to accomplish all we want to do, we would like, if there is any spillover on Thursdays, to extend our sittings to Fridays. In this, we expect co-operation from the Prosecution and the Defence so that our trial will still run through the periods we have slated them to be. On the 16th, that is this Thursday, we are not likely to sit before 11.00 am, because of an earlier pressing administrative matter which we have, and perhaps this Trial Chamber, which is the only one we have, will be used for other business. Today, we will start with oral arguments on the Prosecution's motion to allow certain witnesses to give their testimony by means of videolink conference, which was filed on 26th September. Although we have not received any written response so that we know the reaction of the Defence to the application, we hope in the spirit of general co-operation which we have had all along, the Defence might be able to react to that motion. The Registrar will now call the case so that we can start the business of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-96-21-T, the Prosecutor versus Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And appearances on the part of the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. At the same time, I should like to apologise for not having been informed last Friday and for not being able to attend the unexpectedly convened hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague Mr. Michael Greaves. I should also like to express my apologies because I did not receive on time the invitation to the hearing scheduled for Friday, so please accept my apologies for not being present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic, I am an attorney from Sarajevo, representing Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for appearances. Ms. Residovic and Mr. Olujic need not apologise so profusely, because I do not think you were in any position to be able to respond to that meeting. It was just a gamble, we thought perhaps if you were around then it would have been a good thing for you to have attended. We accept the apologies, although you need not bother with it. Thank you very much. Mr. Niemann, can we hear you on the application?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, on 26th September this year, we filed a motion to allow the witnesses Esad Ramic, Jovan Divjak, Fadil Zebic and Kemal Dzajic to give their testimony by means of videolink conference. The reasons why we sought to do that, if your Honours please, was that at that stage, those witnesses had indicated that they were not prepared to come to The Hague to testify in order to give their evidence and their evidence was important for the Prosecution case, and because of that, we sought to move the Chamber in order to obtain an order to that end. Your Honours, at all stages from then until now, the Prosecution has been endeavouring to persuade each of these witnesses to come forward to The Hague to testify, rather than to give their evidence by videolink. Regrettably, your Honours, we have been unsuccessful to date in persuading them to do that, but unfortunately it goes further, in that in fact the position now stands at this moment, at least two of the witnesses have flatly refused to testify altogether. Whether or not we can bring about a change in that is something that we continue to work upon, but as the position now stands, two of the witnesses refuse to testify, even if an order of the Chamber permitting videolink testimony was to be given. The witness Fadil Zebic has said that he wishes to have nothing further to do with the Tribunal in terms of giving testimony, and refuses to have discussions with our officers in connection with videolink. He had previously indicated that he would have been prepared to testify by videolink, but that he was not prepared to leave his home town. The other witness associated with that witness, Kemal Dzajic, has taken the consistent position all along that if the witness Zebic testifies or comes to The Hague he will too, but if he does not, he will not, so try though we may to separate them on this issue, we have not succeeded in doing that unfortunately as well. I just should say at the moment at this stage, your Honours, the importance of their evidence relates to what they can say about their dealings with bodies that they had received from the Celebici camp, and those bodies being named as persons who are mentioned in the indictment. They work for an organisation which is a funeral company and was responsible for dealing with people who had died and in conducting funerals, so their evidence is important from that point of view. They have provided a certificate relating to these particular people, and it was in relation to that that the Prosecution sought to call them. The witness Esad Ramic had initially -- had at all stages said that he would refuse to come to The Hague, but that he would be prepared to testify. Unfortunately, as things stand at the moment, the Prosecution is doubtful as to whether he will testify either in The Hague or by videolink, even if such an order was made, but we are a little more optimistic that we may be able to either persuade him to change his mind in this regard and indeed we may be able to persuade him to come to The Hague, but we are still pursuing that. I have to say at the moment it is not at all optimistic. Finally, the witness Divjak is probably the least problematic in terms of coming to The Hague. It is a question of timing more than anything else, and it was only -- we only sought to proceed by videolink on the basis that we thought we needed to have his evidence an earlier stage, but I think if we can adjust the timing of when he can come here we may be able to persuade him to come. Again, it is in this state of uncertainty. The two witnesses Ramic and Divjak are important witnesses to the Prosecution because they are military personnel who were actively involved in the area in and about Celebici at the relevant period of time and can testify as to events concerning that and as to who were in positions of authority and who were directing operations in that area at that time, so in varying degrees they are in a position to be able to tell the Chamber about those matters which the Prosecution suggests are very important to those proceedings. So, your Honours, that is the state of affairs at the moment. It is most unfortunate and I should foreshadow that it has the effect that these are the witnesses that we had scheduled for next week, had hoped to be able to take their evidence next week, and regrettably, we have very great difficulties in juggling other witnesses to bring them forward from the week after, should we be unable to secure their attendance next week, so in other words, your Honours, if we can secure their evidence by way of videolink, we will have at least been able to present evidence during the course of next week, if they are prepared to testify according to this process. If, your Honours, we cannot secure their evidence by way of videolink, which we are still hopeful that we may be able to do something in that regard, then the prospect of being able to call evidence next week is in some doubt, although we are constantly working on this in order to overcome the difficulty. So, your Honours, the position is that if we can -- if your Honours are disposed to make an order to grant videolink testimony, we will proceed on the basis of trying to persuade the witness to come to The Hague. If that fails, we believe that we are in a better position to endeavour to persuade them to testify in their home environment, and we would seek to persuade them to testify on that basis, should your Honours be moved to grant the order. But I have to say that even if your Honours were so disposed to grant the order, there is a possibility that nevertheless they will still refuse to testify, and I think it is appropriate and proper that I should tell the court about this now while your Honours are considering the matter. Your Honours, the two bases on which videolink testimony has been granted in the past by this Chamber and other Chamber has been as a consequence of the consideration of the two principal elements of (1), is their evidence important, and in my submission there is no question of the importance of this testimony, and (2), will they refuse to come to The Hague to testify; that is the other pillar on which these orders have been granted in the past. As things stand at the moment, your Honours, there is no question about that. It indeed goes further, it is a question of whether or not they will testify at all, irrespective of whether an order is made, but in my submission, if your Honours were disposed to make the order, then that may well facilitate the process of persuading them to testify. Unless there are other matters, your Honour, that is my submission on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That makes it difficult to ask the Defence to react to this application, from the explanations you have already made. From the explanation it is quite clear at least three of your witnesses are totally unwilling to come forward and there is only one who is likely to do so, or might even come forward, to give evidence in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I acknowledge the difficulty for them in responding to that. Unfortunately, that is the position and I cannot present it any other way than what it is. We are contemplating other measures, perhaps to obtain their attendance here, but that is a course which we may be compelled to follow if we cannot achieve it by way of persuasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That also reduces the chances of the Trial Chamber making an order in such a circumstance, because if all you rely on now is just one witness who might even come forward without a videolink facility, why make a videolink facility for persons who either have totally refused to respond, and which as you are hoping, very slender hope, to persuade to be moved to respond to it. I am sure my colleagues also share my view. It just does not make sense for the Trial Chamber to make an order for such a facility. As correct as your views might be about the necessity of the evidence, that is not enough. If the parties were willing, that will support the application, but at this stage, I do not think it makes any sense to make the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. I cannot present it any other way, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, when I read this application I had doubts that they would even give evidence on videolink in Sarajevo, because the reason given is if they give evidence they will be treated as traitors. The chances of them being treated as traitors would be greater in Sarajevo where they were going to give evidence. I had my suspicion. I thought maybe I said this to you. If they say they will be treated as traitors, if that is so, the chances of them being treated as traitors by the police would be greater in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Very possibly, your Honour. It is only that one of them, at least, Ramic, had said that that is how he wanted to do it, so, notwithstanding it seems illogical, that is what he had said, that was the way he wanted to testify. I cannot put it in any other light. This is how it is, this is how the position is, and I would be misleading the Chamber if I tried to suggest it was any other way. Unfortunately, this is the position we are in. Their evidence, so far as we are concerned, is vital and important, but we are endeavouring to do everything we can to achieve the obtaining of that evidence, but I am afraid I cannot take it further, my Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose you might still keep them in view, if they subsequently change their mind. That may be the only way to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I do appreciate the difficulty, your Honour, and I do appreciate how it would be difficult for the Defence to respond to it, having regard to the uncertainty. I think it is incumbent upon the Prosecution to endeavour to do whatever it can to get the witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will refuse your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we have dealt with this matter, a matter that is not on the agenda but is linked closely to your proposal that we should work intensively for the next four weeks, this also requires a response on the part of the Prosecution so that we on the Defence side might prepare ourselves properly for the next four weeks, for in concluding the hearing in September, the Prosecution told us that out of the list of 23 they intended to call 16, and that they intend to complete their case by the end of this month and in the first week of November at the latest. In the meantime, the Prosecution has informed the Defence of some major changes, first of all that some witnesses would not be coming, so that we had to interrupt our preparations for the cross-examination of those witnesses. Then those witnesses were put back on the list. Then we were informed for a third time that some people on the new list would not be able to come, so that the Defence now is highly confused as to which witnesses the Prosecution intends to call, and when. Will it be in the next four weeks that you have been referring to, your Honour, or will they be the witnesses that are on the list given to us on 9th October, or will they be some other group of witnesses that we are unaware of? My suggestion would be that we ask the Prosecution to be kind enough to tell us exactly which is the final list of witnesses that they intend to hear, and will it be in the next four weeks. We are not asking -- we are just asking who those witnesses are and how many of them there will be, so that we will be able to prepare ourselves in a continuous manner, rather than preparing for a witness for seven days and then having to interrupt those preparations because that witness is scrapped from the list. I hope my comments are in line and that we could hear the Prosecution and my learned colleagues, because this manner of presenting the witness list is causing a great deal of difficulty to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I appreciate entirely the difficulties and inconveniences that have been caused to not only Madam Residovic but to other Defence counsel in relation to this matter. Unfortunately, it is not a matter over which the Prosecution can have much control. Perhaps Madam Residovic, in the spirit -- in pursuit of the truth, and having regard to her considerable contacts in Sarajevo, perhaps may like to utilise those contacts to endeavour to persuade these people to come forward to the Tribunal and testify, on the basis that they would not be regarded as traitors but would be co-operating and participating in pursuit of the truth of the matter, which I am sure Madam Residovic is as committed to as all of us in this Chamber. So, I invite her to do so when she next returns to Sarajevo, so that we can endeavour to have these people here to testify, which I am sure would be for the benefit of all. But unfortunately, so far as our efforts are concerned, we are doing everything within our power to have these people here. We have written to Madam Residovic on 9th October; we have set out our position as best we can and indicated it as best we can. Indeed, it may change -- it probably will change, but this is our best estimate at the moment. The only solace that I can offer to her is that when she is in an equally difficult position herself perhaps the Prosecution might extend to her the consideration that we would ask to have extended to us, having regard to the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know whether you have actually responded to Ms. Residovic's complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do believe, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I understand her to mean that she wants an actual list of the witnesses you intend to call from now until the Prosecution completes its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: She has that, your Honour, so why she is now raising this matter, I do not know. She has a list as of 9th October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that correct? You have the list which the Prosecution intends to call, a list of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not understand the document sent to us by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has listed three witnesses for this week and seven witnesses whom they will call, but this differs completely from the list of 23, then from the list of 16, then from the changes in the list made between 22nd September and 9th October, so my first question is: is this the final list of witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call or not, because that cannot be seen from the letter. Are they the people who will be called in the next four weeks that you, your Honour, have spoken of? I wish to thank the Prosecutor for thinking that I have an important position in Sarajevo. I will be very pleased if at some stage of the proceedings in the interest of the proceedings I will be able to assist the Trial Chamber, but I do not feel it my duty to assist the Prosecution in the same way. However, since the question has been put, but not as an answer to my question, I must say that some of the witnesses on the list, like Pasalic, Esad Ramic, never wanted to have any contact with the Defence, so that I think it is up to the Prosecution to prove its case, to find the witnesses and to bring them to the Tribunal. I wish to repeat that the Defence of Mr. Delalic is not questioning the number of witnesses, we just wish to know who they will be and when they will come. If this is the final list, then we know where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I cannot assist Madam Residovic any more than perhaps to read out the letter and to say what we mean by it. We give the list of witnesses that we intended to call this week, Witness J, Witness R and Arif Pasalic. It does not look as though we are going to be able to secure the attendance of Arif Pasalic as things stand at the moment. We then go on to say in our letter: "As you know, we continue to have difficulties in scheduling our witnesses. We have listed below the witnesses that we anticipate we will be able to call in the upcoming weeks. We will notify you when we have additional details concerning their appearance. Given the small number of remaining witnesses, we assume that you will be ready for these witnesses whenever they are called. We are also continuing our efforts to have other witnesses appear and we will notify you of those witnesses when we are successful. "The position as it now stands at the moment is that we only have seven witnesses that we were reasonably optimistic about and that even that may be less. We are not very optimistic that we will be able to obtain any more. This is notwithstanding the fact that our ambitions were high when we advised the Chamber of all the outstanding pieces of evidence that we wanted to put forward. Unfortunately, we have reached the stage where we have had considerable difficulties in this regard."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this concludes the dispute about the number of witnesses. Where are we this morning with regard to your witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have a witness your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We do have a witness, your Honour, for this morning. It would be Witness J, and if your Honours are ready, the Prosecution would be ready to proceed with Witness J, who is in the witness room. He is a protected witness so we would need to close the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is ready, I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, there was another matter that was scheduled for an oral hearing, having to do with an ex parte communication. Does the court not want to hear that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which is that, under Rule 46?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The Rule 46 motion, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have dealt with it differently. We will send it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise for just five minutes to get the place ready for the witness. (10.45 am) (A short break) (10.50 am) (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness. WITNESS J (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May the witness be seated, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he can. Examined by MS. McHENRY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you your Honours. Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name and identity not be released to the public or the media and that your face not be shown to the public or media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand that the judges have granted your request and thus that you will be known publicly as "Mr. J". Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would ask that, with the assistance of the usher, a piece of paper with a name be shown to the witness, and I will just ask that you look at that and just say yes or no if that is your correct name. Then it can be given to the Registrar for the record. Sir, is that your actual name? You should not say it, sir. You should not say your name. You should just say whether or not it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you are now 46 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May 1992, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1992 I lived in Bradina, which is near Konjic. It is between Konjic and Sarajevo. It is about 12 kilometres from Konjic, going in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Bradina and I had my own business, I had a restaurant, I had two stores, I had my own slaughter house, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trained as a butcher also, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was trained as a butcher, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of May in 1992, sir, was there any kind of attack or military action in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time after the action in Bradina when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I surrendered in Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far away from Konjic or from Bradina is Pazaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is approximately 20 kilometres, 20 some kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate date that it was when you surrendered, or do you know approximately how many days after the attack on Bradina it was when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about four days. It was four to five days, maybe. I do not know exactly. I am not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, approximately four or five days, had you been in hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you surrendered, where were you imprisoned, initially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I surrendered in a barracks, I think it was a military barracks. It was called Krupa, and from there, I was taken to Pazaric, to a headquarters of theirs, and from there I was transferred to the silo in Tarcin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long a time did you remain in prison in the silos in Tarcin, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was two days, that is what I think. I think that was two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you brought after those two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After two days, I was taken to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, later on I am going to ask you sort of in more detail questions, but just for now, so that the judges can have an overview, can you say approximately how long it was that you stayed in Celebici, overall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether I think I spent about four months in Celebici. Then I was moved to the sports hall at Musala, that was how it was called, the Musala Sports Hall, and then I was again taken back to Celebici from Musala and then I was let go. The same day when I was brought back from Musala to Celebici was the day I was released from Celebici, the same night, that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the beginning when you were first brought to Celebici in early June, how many other prisoners arrived with you in Celebici at that same time as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with me, I think it was about six prisoners, five or six, six as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of their names, and if so, would you please just tell us the names of the prisoners who came with you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Branislav Mrkajic, Borivoje Mrkajic, Dragan Mrkajic, Andjelko Kuljanin, so Andjelko Kuljanin, Dragan Mrkajic, Brana Mrkajic, Branislav, Andjelko Kuljanin, Borivoje Mrkajic, Gojko Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, would you please tell the judges exactly what happened once you were brought to Celebici, and I would ask that you speak slowly in case I need to interrupt or ask any clarifying questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were brought to Celebici, we were brought in a bus of a sort from Tarcin, and this bus was stopped in Bradina and then in Bradina. They tied us with some wire, then they threatened to kill us, then it was parked right in front of the house where my business was, where I lived, Jasmin Guska, Sevrin Niksic was there, I know them personally and I saw them personally there. They would tell me, why did you run away, you had so much money, you have millions of Deutschmarks, so why did you run away, fuck your Chetnik mother, and so he ordered us to be tied and then this -- they brought this wire and then pliers and that is what they used on us and then they were going to go to take us to some warehouse and shoot us. But anyway, we were ordered to stop, it was Gojko, Dragan and then myself, I was number three, one behind the other, so somebody ordered us to stop and some Divsa, I remember that well, Divsa was from Konjic, he was a former husband of Jasmina Dzumhur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can, can I just take you to the time when you were actually brought to Celebici and can you tell us, once the vehicle brought you into Celebici, can you tell us exactly what happened once the vehicle arrived in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the vehicle arrived, this bus, when it arrived in Celebici, then they placed us against a wall of the infirmary and they said, "hands up" and then "throw everything out of your pockets, whatever you have". At that point, Pavo was there also, Mr. Pavo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Pavo, can you just give us the full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic, called Zdravko now, in fact Zdravko Mucic, called Pavo, but in the camp, everyone called him Pavo for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, sir, with what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they said, "take everything out" and I remember well, there was a Macic near, a man called Macic, he was working as some scribe there in that command and this Macic took stuff away from me. I had a sort of cap, it had like a little tuft like children had, and then he said "throw that on the ground" and there was -- somebody said, "take those hats again" and I thought that he was saying to both of us, because there was another one who had a hat and then they said, "your hat looks like a particular kind of hat", and they started putting it back on his head, whereas mine, they did not. Then Pavo came and said, "he has a lot of money, lot of money" and then they kicked me a little bit. Gojko who was there, who was beaten up in Bradina, he was all bloodied, so they put some kind of a net on his head, and there was some Dzajic, some Nuta there, and I heard when this Dzajic said, "do not beat them, because they have already gotten enough". Then they called out this Boro Mrkajic a couple of minutes later, they said "step forward" and he did and he said, "I saw you in Bradina, you were running down a road, I could have killed you, I was commander up there", so he was telling him that he was the commander of this unit, that was coming down from the Boro Mrkajic, "I am told you are some kind of an army, but you are absolutely no army".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who was it who was talking to Boro Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Nuta, that was what he was called, Nuta. I know him personally, I know that he worked for the municipal government for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see if any -- were any valuables taken off you or did you see any valuables taken from other persons once they arrived in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taking things away in the camp, actually number 9, chains and watches, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first arrived at the camp, when you have told us about, and there were these people including Nuta and Mr. Mucic and I believe Masic, were any valuables taken off you or the other prisoners at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody had to turn over whatever they had, and they said, "if you did not do it, you will die, if we find anything on you". And then everybody was just throwing down on the ground whatever they had on them. I do remember well that Macic personally took some things, he worked as a scribe, he was used as a clerk there, he was shortish. I did not know him before, but I know that his last name was Macic and that he -- I know him from then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. Mucic address you individually at all when you were first brought to the camp and if so, would you please just state exactly your interaction with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said, he said, "you finally arrived". I remember we were there at the infirmary, I was on the left, not from the gate but looking towards the wall. Here was the infirmary, I was over here and then he came from behind and he said, "okay, we can get a lot of money out of you". That is all he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please, what happened after you and the other persons were standing there and had to give up your valuables. What happened next? Would you please continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, somebody gave the order to take us to number 6, and I heard Mucic's voice, he said "no, not to number 6, to number 9", and then when they brought us in front of number 9, the guards were in two lines and then they beat us as we passed down between them, and then when I got in, there were a lot of beaten up people and there was blood on the walls, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you first got to the camp and you indicated that people started to beat you until Dzajic said to stop and when you were actually going into the tunnel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic present during any of the occasions when you and the other prisoners were beaten at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not present up there. He was not up there, because he stayed down at a command building, but I think he could have seen it from there. He was not up there, he was not up in front of that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say not up there, do you mean he was not up there in front of tunnel 9 when the prisoners were beaten as they went into the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were taken up there by some guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned, when you talk about Mr. Mucic, do you remember whether or not he was wearing a uniform or civilian clothes on that day you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Mucic's position, if any, in the camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have that position the entire time you were imprisoned in Celebici, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe -- you indicate that you were first placed in tunnel number 9. Can you describe for the judges the conditions in tunnel number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In tunnel number 9, the conditions were very very bad. It was a concrete structure that had a decline, there was -- at the bottom there was a door, a big metal door and up there also with a small bar, so the conditions were terrible. The prisoners who were already there went to urinate down at the bottom, but some people could not go to the bathroom for 30 or 40 days even. Everybody was beaten up and they were almost disfigured from all this, so the conditions were very bad. The walls were bloody. There were no bathroom facilities, so people went down to the bottom of number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were in tunnel 9 -- first of all, how long did you stay imprisoned in tunnel 9, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there for a long time, I think about three months, maybe more, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in tunnel number 9, sir, can you please describe what kind of food you received and what kind of water you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was practically no food, I think that within 24 hours, we would get something like a few grammes of bread and we suffered for those -- that first period for some time, so we did not get anything for 72 hours sometimes 24 hours. It was like 5 grammes of bread, so it was just barely enough that one would get a tiniest piece, so the conditions were very poor, so that we almost starved. We could not even move in the end. I weighed 95 kilos when I was brought in and then, when I finally left the camp, I weighed 58 kilos, so it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of drinking water, sir, did you have in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of water it was, but it was in some kind of a bucket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of washing facilities did you have when you were in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None. At first, they would not let us wash or shave, so that sometimes, we had cramps, so we were unable to move our hands much. They would not let us bathe or shave and then after some time, they took us out and washed us down with a hose, then they locked us up again in the concrete, but there was all kinds of maltreatment, and even this hose, it was so powerful that an elderly man would fall down from the strength of the water coming out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that when you arrived in tunnel number 9 there already were other prisoners in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many prisoners were kept in the tunnel when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think more than 30, because after me, somebody called Marko and Milomir came and then afterwards Susic, so that I think roughly there was about 40 of us in all, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where approximately, sir, was your place in the tunnel? How far away from the door to the tunnel were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not far from the door, I think there were five or six men between me and the door. I remember some of them. Anyway, I was not far from the door, I was very close, right up front. We were all very cramped, because people were trying to move away from the dirt at the bottom of the tunnel as much as possible, from the filth, so that we were crowded up front. There was Rajko Mrkajic, then Desko Mrkajic, somebody Nikola, an elderly man, Mrkajic also, then Milenko. Who else was there; Nikola, Rajko, Desko, Velimir Mrkajic, Nikola Mrkajic, Andelko Kuljanin, Milenko Kuljanin and then me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were in Celebici, were you ever interrogated or questioned in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times we were questioned and interrogated and taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us -- please, to the judges, about how exactly an official interrogation, how that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time we were questioned was only a couple of days after we were incarcerated, two or three days. They took us out of number 9, then they told us to sit on the road, and then as the names were called out, we went down to the command building for some kind of interrogation. While I was in number 9, I was taken out several times to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, staying with the time that you were called -- you were brought out and sat on the road and then were called into the command building; can you tell us approximately how long your interrogation lasted and if you know who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated by my former physics professor, Miro Stenek, who more recently before the war did not work as a professor, as a teacher, but worked in the SUP in Konjic, and then also another Muslim, I know that for sure, I cannot remember his name, I know that he was a big man, the two of them questioned me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the interrogation, I was not mistreated. I saw Delic in the corridor, he would peep through the door, but he did not mistreat me. He did not touch me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after your interrogation, were you ever told by anyone if you had been placed in any kind of category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the interrogation, I had no idea about any categories, but when I was transferred to the infirmary, somebody called Ismeta said that there were nine categories. That was the first time I heard of it and she said that such and such were in the first category and you are in number 2 and you are in number 3, so she would tell us which category we had been put into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Ismeta's function at the camp? Did she work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that she did, she had some kind of a role of secretary, I think. She was quite decent, she did not mistreat anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if she told you in particular anything about what category you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, each one of us asked her when the others were not there. She would come in and sometimes she would even take detainees to cut some wood at her mother's place. She did not give the impression of any extremist. And then we would talk to her and then I asked, "look at that list, please, and tell us", and then she would come and say, for instance, "you are in the first category and this one is in the second category", and then we would discuss amongst ourselves the existence of those categories. She personally would come and say, "you are in the first category, you are in the second and that one is in the third", and so on. We were all somehow up to the third category. This was in the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember, did she ever tell you in particular what category you were in, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she told me, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What category did she tell you that you had been placed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were in Celebici, were you yourself ever mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times, terribly mistreated, so that after one of those occasions, I could not sit or lie down for three days. But I was mistreated several times. Sometimes Delic or the others would not be present and sometimes they were present when this mistreatment took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask, starting with the first incident you remember, can you please tell the judges exactly what happened with respect to the first incident you remember where you were mistreated, and I will remind you to please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One case of mistreatment occurred -- are you thinking of the interrogation or the interrogation and mistreatment? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking about times where you were physically mistreated, and if it occurred as part of an interrogation, please explain that to the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, I was mistreated once when a team, some kind of a team arrived, but this was later. Before that, I was taken out and mistreated not so badly and then one night about 9.00 in the evening somebody called Kravar and his group of men, his guards, they lined me up against the wall as you go out of number 9, there was a big wall but not at that wall, another small wall which was leaning against number 9, so when you go out of number 9 and when you turn right right there, next to the door. I was mistreated then, terribly. There was an Edo called "MUP", they knocked some teeth out then and then they demanded "where is your money, you will confess, you must confess". They swore at me, "you will admit to us". At that moment I was facing the wall, they beat me terribly, I had to lean my hands against the wall and then I saw I was about to fall and I turned round and I saw with my own eyes this Kravar who hit me with his fist in the face, and as it was nighttime, I saw him pushing his way into the group, and then an Edo "MUP" came up and said "here you are, kill me" and he cocked the gun as if it was loaded but I did not know if it was loaded or not, and then he said "here you are, here is the rifle, kill me" and I said I could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for a minute. First of all, with this person you are saying -- let me just see -- what was this person's nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kravar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned someone who was called "MUP" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Edo "MUP". He was the one handed me the rifle, he was the one who wanted to give me the rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before we get to when you were handed the rifle, can you say how it was that they were mistreating you? Can you tell us approximately how many there guards doing this, approximately what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a number of them, it was nighttime so I could not count them, I think there were more than ten of them, they were there, they made me face the wall and they started beating me terribly, rifle butts, kicking me, all kinds of things, bats against my back, my bottom, the lower part of my body and they beat me so badly that I saw I was about to fall. When I saw that I was about to fall, I turned round and when I turned round, I saw, though it was dark, I saw Kravar punching me in the eye and he had pushed his way into the group. When he did that, Edo "MUP" said to me, "here is the rifle", he loaded it and handed it to me, and I said I could not and he cursed my mother and said "if you cannot kill me, go and kill yourself" and again he loaded the gun and he kept handing it to me, but I was afraid and I was exhausted and my heart was beating terribly, I was unable to do anything and he said "take it, take it" and I had to take it into my hand. I remember it was a semi-automatic rifle, something like that, and it was a long one, and he held it out and he said "point the barrel towards you and hold the trigger". I was holding it like this (indicates) and he put the barrel against my chest and I was confident that there was a bullet, but I moved it a little bit to the side exactly where my heart was beating so that I would not suffer and if it killed me then I would die immediately and I did pull the trigger, but there was no bullet. Then again they pushed me down and continued beating me and threw me into number 9 so that for three days I could not sit, I could not lie, I could not do anything. However, I forgot to mention that somebody at that moment said, somewhere behind the group, somebody said "that is enough" and by the voice, I thought it was Delic, but it was not Delic, but it was somebody called Ismet who was also some kind of a leader of the guards and when I was transferred to Musala. I always thought it had been Delic, but when I got to Musala, this Ismet said "you see, if it had not been for me, they would have killed you. Did you hear me say 'that is enough'?" So that is how I knew it was Ismet who had said "that is enough" and not Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did the people who were beating you on this occasion, did they all work in the camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they were all working. There were ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That has been asked and answered. He said it was nighttime and he could not see anyone, so how could he know whether they worked in the camp or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was nighttime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the people whose names you have identified, did those people work in the camp, were they guards in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Edo and Kravar and the others, the people who were beating me, is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were working in the camp and I know them very well and I know they were there, because they were right next to me, 20 centimetres away from me when I turned around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, do you not think we should break and return at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think that is right. Thank you, your Honour. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we continue, perhaps I might --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I might want to have some clarification from Mr. Niemann. It is almost certain that you have no witnesses for us next week? We would want to know what arrangement you are making for that period, if you have any of the expert witnesses to swap for that period, or what other arrangements you do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, perhaps it is better that I explain what we are doing so that that way it may assist in understanding what might happen. We have had, I might just say, we have had a mission down in the relevant area all last week, endeavouring to get these people in for next week. That failed. It was not successful in achieving that. We are considering, it is perhaps a little premature for me to mention now, but we are considering making an application to the Chamber for a subpoena, and that is in the process of being drawn at the moment, and that would go off this week, with the intention that the witnesses would be compelled to appear next week, should your Honours be disposed to grant that. With respect to bringing witnesses from the week after back a week earlier, there is a number of problems with that; one of the problems is that one of the witnesses particularly simply cannot make it at all. The other witness has said that -- he is an expert witness, and he has said it would be very difficult for him to make it and has basically ruled out the possibility of being able to come at that time. At least in respect of those two witnesses there are some difficulties. There is possibly another third witness that we had contemplated calling that we are endeavouring to bring forward for that week, so it is regrettably in a very unsatisfactory and unstable situation, but we are hoping that as the week progresses we may be in a better position to inform the Chamber of our successes or failures in this regard. Perhaps I might indicate that we only have two witnesses for this week, but we have the issue of the documents that were seized by the Austrian police yet outstanding in terms of a tender. I expect that to be a rather lengthy and drawn out exercise so I am not concerned, if we sit through to Thursday, that there be any difficulty this week in using the time available. Our concern is being able to ensure that we can sit next week and to be able to use that time, but I regret, your Honour, I cannot be of much more assistance than to simply tell you of our progress, what we are doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are your difficulties. I just want to know how we could use next week so that we will be sure as to how to organise the time we have and the outstanding matters which are likely to come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is our wish, your Honour, to use it by calling evidence and we are doing everything we can to see that we can do that. I am hoping later in the week, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The subpoena experience is a fairly long drawn one. We do not know what would happen even if it is pursued. All right, we just hope that you make your best efforts so that we would not waste time unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am very conscious of that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may now wish to carry on with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I heard Mr. Niemann suggest that they only have two witnesses for this week and we have been advised of three. Now I am confused, I do not know whether they have three or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As things stand at the moment, we have two. We had intended to have three, we spoke to the third witness, we issued the -- the Victims and Witnesses Unit have issued airline tickets and everything, but the witness refuses to come. At this stage, the witness is not coming, so we only have two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is important we know which one it is so we can prepare for the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is not coming, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From your report earlier on, I had an inkling that he is not likely to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, with respect to the incident you described just before the break with Kravar and Edo, can you give any approximate idea of when this happened, even the month it happened, or if you can say approximately how long you had been at the camp or if it was at the beginning or the end of the time you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the beginning, during the initial part of my stay in the camp. It was in the very beginning. This was the night I think, the night following the day when we were kept in a manhole and then after we were released it was the following night that it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Why do we not then, sir -- why do you not please describe what happened the day that you were kept in a manhole. Would you please just describe what exactly happened and I would ask that you start at the beginning and go slowly step by step, to make sure that everyone understands what happened, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, there were about 40 of us in this number 9, and we were split into two groups, one group was taken to the manhole one day and then the next group the following day, so in my group, I think it was about 17 of us. We were taken from number 9 and taken down a road, it was a road there, and we were brought to this manhole. We did not know where we were going, where they were taking us, we did not know that this manhole existed. However, before this manhole, one group brought us there and on the other side, there were cars and then we were going down there and then off to the side there were these guards and then in between, each one of us had to pass two men, I think -- one I think was called Rambo and I think that the other one was called Ture, and they were holding some sticks and we were supposed to pass between them and as we were passing by, they hit us. They both hit me on the knee, in the knee area. I staggered -- I fell down to my hands and then they said, "up, up there, off to the right", so there were some kind of stairs up and there was an opening at the top, and I think that Delic and Zenga were up there, but before I arrived, five or six people were already down in the manhole, so when I finally jumped down in, I was helped by these people who were already there, so we were all in that manhole and then 15 or 20 minutes later, Pavo came and brought Zara out of that, and we were all then kept there, I do not know, there were some wheels there, more like valves, and I remember there was like a staircase that were sort of like a wire or a cable type. We were kept there for about nine hours and after -- there was a lid up on top and then they -- that was all closed and after about nine hours, people started suffocating, because there was no air. Then after nine hours, one prisoner went up there to check that lid. However, at that time, to push it up, Kravar was there, and he opened up there lid after nine hours, but I think there was maybe another 15 minutes, had we been kept there another 15 minutes we would have all died, because you could not breathe any more, and it was like the ribcage was bursting, and so Kravar then opened it. I was lying on the ground and my mouth was next to the concrete, so we were all on top of one another and if somebody was sitting down, he was worse off than the one who had their mouth next to the concrete, so I kept my mouth next to the concrete all the time, but you felt like your ribcage was bursting, and then when he opened this lid, he said, "I am going to throw in a grenade" and when this air came in, we all said, "just throw it in". We would have preferred for him to have thrown in a grenade than to go on like that. Then they brought us out of there and then they lined us up. One had to be in front and then the next one behind him with the arm on the other man's shoulder and then they took us down that road, so a person was in front of me and I had to place my arm on his shoulder and the next prisoner on my shoulder and then we walked down that road and we walked towards the command building and that went on for a long time. He said, "who started the war?", and then we were silent and then he would say "Karadzic" and we had to repeat, "Karadzic".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for a minute. Do you know, this time you were put in the manhole, are you able to say whether or not this was in the first week or the first month or the first several months that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was not a long time after we were brought to the camp, it was not long. It was a short period of time. I think a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of approximately where this manhole was? Was it very close to the tunnel, was it towards the gate house, was it towards the other direction? Can you give us an idea of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not that close to the tunnel and it was not in the direction of the gate house, it was the opposite, so you came out of the tunnel like this (indicates) and there was a road and then you turned and you walked towards that manhole. So it was not towards the gate, but to the other side, the opposite side. I think it was at the far end of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate that when you went to the -- first of all, let me ask, with the assistance of the usher, that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1, which is the book of photographs, and I would specifically be referring to photos 38, 39 and 40, which are on pages 29 and 30 of Prosecution Exhibit 1. If they could be put on the ELMO and shown to the witness? (Handed). The witness is now being shown photograph 38. If the usher could also now show the witness photos 39 and 40.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you do that, sir, I am sorry, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the manhole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those the steps that you said that you had to go up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you say from the camp was on top of this structure? Were there any guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean at the lid?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Delic and Zenga were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown photographs 39 and 40. Sir, do you recognise what these photos are, photographs 39 and 40?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 39 is the photograph of the lid, that is where you enter that manhole, and the other photograph is the steps or the ladder rungs going in and the first one is the lid at the top, where you stepped in. This is this iron bars that were the rungs, where you would go down into the manhole. That I can say with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, usher. Sir, you indicated that when you went down into the manhole, there were already about five other prisoners who were down in the manhole, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That is correct. I just slid down, but there were five or six of them there already at the bottom, so they held me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners placed in this manhole after you? In other words, how many prisoners were placed in this manhole altogether, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 17, but as we were locked when Zara was taken out, nobody was brought in in addition to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned Zara. Was Zara another prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also with us in the camp in number 9, in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Zara's full name, if you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zara Mrkajic, Zarko Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have indicated that you saw Delic and Zenga present there. First of all, do you know the full name of Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic's position in the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was Pavo's deputy, I think he was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise -- had you seen Mr. Delic before you got to the camp? In other words, did you know him or recognise him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see him occasionally down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you would see him occasionally, you mean before you got to the camp you had seen him occasionally, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have previously talked about Mr. Mucic. Had you seen Mr. Mucic before you got to the camp and did you know who he was before you got to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him before, Mr. Mucic, and I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Zenga. What was Zenga's position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga was a guard in the camp, he had a duty of a guard in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Zenga from before you were in the camp or did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him not well at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, what was -- first of all, do you know if Zenga is a real name or if it is a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that most prisoners knew him as Zenga. Later on, I found out that his name was Landzo, but he was called Zenga by all inmates and he was known as Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, was he known to you as Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what Zenga looked like, during the time he was a guard in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean how he looked physically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not very tall, he was fairly young, he was shortish, he had a very high-pitched voice, almost like a feminine voice, that is how the pitch was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only person you heard called Zenga when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not hear anybody else being called that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, going back to the manhole, when you were placed in the manhole, were all 16 or 17 prisoners kept in the manhole for the -- other than Zara -- kept in the manhole for the nine hours that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all except for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being placed in the manhole, did you see anyone else from the camp besides Mr. Delic and Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was put in there, I could not see anybody, it was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir, at the time that you were brought to the manhole and before you were actually put inside down in the manhole, do you remember anyone else who was present besides Mr. Delic and Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were guards who were lined up to the left of us. After about ten minutes, I heard some voices and I think there was even some laughter and there was some shooting later on. I do not know what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long had Zara been in the manhole before Mr. Mucic removed Zara from the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 15 minutes, after we were all inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the camp, was Zara treated like the other prisoners or was there anything different about how Zara was treated, or his position as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very different. He almost did not look like a prisoner. He would walk around, he was with the guards, and with Pavo and with others; in other words, he was almost like free. He would talk about what was going on and here and there, when he would come in. He said that he would be exchanged, but then he would lie. He was free, basically. He had different treatment, he ate well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate that Mr. Mucic removed Zara. Had Mr. Mucic been present when you and the other prisoners been placed in the manhole, or is the first time when you saw or heard him when he removed Zara from the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, I think he was there. I think he was there in a corner, to the left. I do not know, it was a difficult moment for us, because we thought that we were going to get killed, they were going to throw us there and kill us, because when we were passing between those two, they were beating us with these poles, as they could, and we had the feeling that we were going to be thrown in and killed there. That was the feeling we all had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first placed in the manhole? Was it during the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were saying what happened when you left the manhole after eight or nine hours. Can you just please continue with what happened when you were finally let out of the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were finally released, we came down the steps and then we had to line up one behind the other with one hand on the shoulder of the man in front. There were quite a number of guards there, and then someone known as Maca, actually there were two brothers, Maca was the older brother of the two, they were both guards and this Maca had a flat in Konjic, right next door to me. This one who was in command, and his brother was there too, and they took us towards the command building, we passed building number 6, and then on towards the command building and then he would say, "who started the war?", we were all quiet and he said, "Karadzic", and we had to repeat after him, "Karadzic", and he says, "who is the best man in the world?", and he says "Alija" and we have to repeat after him. He says, "who is homosexual?", and there is somebody called Siljivo who is a shepherd, and we would say, "Siljivo", and Siljivo will say, "I will fuck your Chetnik mothers", and it went on like that. They were mistreating us in various ways, we had to walk around the compound and then we were locked up again where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in tunnel number 9 that you were locked up after you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was outside and then afterwards we were locked up in tunnel number 9 from where we had been taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know it was Mr. Mucic who removed Zara from the manhole 15 or 20 minutes after you and the others were placed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could hear laughter, jokes being made with Zara and there was even some shooting I think, some kind of celebration, I think. We could hear them talking and this kind of laughter and joking, so I think there was some pistol firing as well. They were pretending actually to take him out and kill him, so we thought maybe he had been killed, but in fact this was all a joke, it was all pretence, they were laughing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have said it was -- how do you know that it was Mr. Mucic who ordered or directed that Zara be removed from the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because Zara himself told us, and I know that he was there, we could hear the voice and the words exchanged. I heard him saying, ordering that he should be taken out. I heard him saying that Zara should come out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "him", are you referring to Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you now please tell us about the next incident that you remember when you were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mistreated several times, I do not know what exactly I should say. Once they took me to be hanged, to a hangar. I remember that. I think that this was agreed because if it had not been agreed in advance that they should let me go, they probably would have hung me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please, with respect to the incident where they took you to be hanged, can you please just tell the judges exactly what happened and I will ask that you go slowly and start from the beginning. Where were you detained at the time? Who came for you? Can you just please -- first of all, this incident, where were you detained at the time where this hanging incident happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was still being held in number 9 at the time, and then Delic came one day and he called my name and told me to come out, and he was holding a big rope in his hand, a big rope, and like a kind of knife and he said, "come out", and I went out, and then they ordered me to turn around, and go behind number 9 to the right, and then somebody ordered, "load the gun", but a man was going backwards in front of me, backwards. I know this man. He used to give tickets in the cinema, so I know him. I cannot remember his name, but I know that he sold tickets at the cinema. I have forgotten his name in the meantime. Then they brought me there, and when they did that, I think it was Delic who said, "climb up there, two of you" and then two of them climbed up, and they let down a rope, they tied me round the neck, and it was rather loose, it was not tight, and then I looked at the guard who was in front of me who held a rifle pointed at my forehead, he was close to me and I looked at him, and he sort of waved his hand, saying, "you are done for", the gesture meant. Then after that, Delic was behind me, I could not see him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you. In the beginning, when you said Mr. Delic came with a rope in his hand, were you able to see Mr. Delic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes of course, when I walked up to him. He was standing here and I came from here, from the door (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then can you describe approximately where it was that they took you, sir, where in relation to the tunnel? Was it a building, was it a structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to a hangar, and this hangar, because when I came out of number 9 I went to the right along a path, and then they took me to a hangar which was again to the right of the road, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would ask that the witness be shown photo number 44 from Prosecution Exhibit 1, which is on page 32. (Handed). I know it is not the best quality, sir, but can you tell me if you recognise what is shown in photo 44?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it. That is the hangar, yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, usher. That will be all. So please continue. You had said that -- please continue with what happened to you. You indicate that the rope had been placed around your neck. Was the rope placed anywhere else besides around your neck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And round my chest (indicates) here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling, and I think you were at the present where someone was pointing a rifle at you and you say Mr. Delic was behind you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please continue with what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he said, "what is your last wish?" I did not know what to say in case I said something wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who asked you what your last wish was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I said, "my only wish is to see my children", and then he said, and the other guard said, "you will never see them, because these are the last moments of your life", and they started pulling me up, and when they pulled me up a little, they asked me, "where is the money?", where is this, where is that, mostly about money. I said I did not know. Actually, as I was hanging by the neck, I could not speak, I started choking. Then they let me down a bit again, and then they said, "where is the money?"
